steps.title: How would you describe them?
steps.html:
A forensic artist drew two portraits of the same woman. He never saw her. The difference between the two pictures became one of the most-watched advertisements ever made.

A  The set-up was unusual. A forensic artist — the kind normally employed by the police to draw a suspect from a witness’s description — sat behind a curtain. He could not see the woman on the other side. She described her own face to him: shoulder-length hair, a fringe, a rather large chin. He drew what he heard. Then a stranger who had met her that morning described the same face, and he drew it again.

B  The two portraits were put side by side. Almost every time, the self-described face was older, heavier and sadder than the one the stranger described. One woman had called her own face “a lot more closed off, and fatter, sadder too”. The stranger’s version had softer eyes and a slightly open mouth. The women were shown both drawings together, and several of them cried.

C  The film went round the world within days, and psychologists were quick to point out that it was not an experiment. The women were not chosen at random, the strangers were prompted to be kind, and a commercial company paid for all of it. None of that, though, explains why the film worked. It worked because the gap it showed was one almost everybody recognises: we are far more precise about our own faults than about anybody else’s.

D  Research on self-perception supports the general point, if not the advertisement. People describing themselves use noticeably more negative detail than people describing a stranger. They are also far more specific: a double chin, thin eyebrows, a nose that is slightly crooked. Strangers describe in much broader strokes — blonde, quite slim, well-built, friendly-looking — and rarely mention the features that the person themselves has been thinking about for twenty years.

E  Some of this is simply information. You have looked at your own face many thousands of times more often than anyone else has, so you notice smaller changes: the grey coming in, the hair going. A stranger has three seconds and a general impression. It is not that they are being generous. They are working with far less detail, and detail is where dissatisfaction lives.

F  The advertisement ended with a line telling women they were more beautiful than they thought. It is a nice sentiment, and it is also a company selling soap. The more interesting conclusion is smaller and harder to package: the face other people see is not more flattering than yours. It is simply less examined — and by far the most critical description of you that exists anywhere is the one you carry around in your own head.

Written for this course. Based on published accounts of the Real Beauty Sketches campaign (2013) and on research into self-perception.
